findings: Lateral radiograph of the foot and ankle with adequate technical quality. All 6 agents independently assessed the image. Cortical margins of the distal tibia, talus, calcaneus, and metatarsals are intact with no visible fracture lines, cortical step-offs, or disruptions confirmed across independent agent reviews. Joint spaces (tibiotalar and subtalar) appear preserved. No dislocation or gross malalignment. Calcaneal angular measurements (Böhler 45.3°, Gissane 104.8°) are outside normal ranges but all agents agreed these discrepancies likely reflect automated landmark placement error rather than true pathology, supported by intact calcaneal cortex on unsharp mask and anterior calcaneus crop views. An initial solo finding by Agent_05 of a possible cuboid/lateral midfoot abnormality was independently evaluated by Agents 03, 05, and 06 and refuted — the apparent trabecular disruption is consistent with superimposition of overlapping tarsal bones in the single lateral projection, not a genuine lesion. Kager's fat pad triangle is preserved, suggesting absence of acute posterior ankle pathology. Soft tissue contour analysis shows no focal swelling over the midfoot. Plantar calcaneal surface appears smooth without clear spur formation. A faint linear density in the distal tibial metaphysis noted by Agent_06 was not confirmed on enhanced views and is likely an artifact of overlapping fibular cortex.
impression: No acute fracture or dislocation identified on this single lateral view of the foot and ankle. Bony alignment appears maintained. The single-view limitation is significant — occult fractures (navicular, 5th metatarsal base, lateral malleolus), ligamentous injuries, and subtle joint incongruity cannot be excluded without AP and oblique views. The automated calcaneal angle measurements should not be considered diagnostic due to landmark uncertainty.
limitations: Single lateral view only — AP, mortise, and oblique views are required for complete evaluation. No clinical history or mechanism of injury provided. No contralateral comparison available. Image is a PNG (8-bit raster) derived from the original DICOM, limiting post-processing capabilities. Automated calcaneal angle measurements have inherent landmark placement uncertainty. Several processing outputs had methodological issues: the cuboid texture analysis compared bone to background rather than to a valid calcaneal control ROI; the distal tibia enhanced crop was insufficiently sized (94x172px); the plantar calcaneus crop ROI was misplaced. All 6 agents use the same model (qwen3.6-27b), so agreement represents consistency between independent runs, not cross-model validation.

findings: Lateral radiograph of the elbow and proximal forearm. The distal humerus, elbow joint (humeroulnar and humeroradial articulations), proximal radius and ulna, and partial distal forearm are visualized. Cortical margins of the distal humerus, radial head, olecranon, and proximal forearm bones appear intact and continuous with no visible fracture lines, step-offs, or cortical disruptions. Joint spaces are preserved and uniform without evidence of dislocation or subluxation. The anterior fat pad in the coronoid fossa is visible as a thin triangular radiolucency, which is a normal finding. The posterior fat pad is not visualized, which is the expected normal finding and carries high negative predictive value for occult intra-articular fracture. No visible soft tissue swelling, calcification, or foreign body. No periosteal reaction or abnormal bone density is identified. Alignment of the radius and ulna with the distal humerus is appropriate for a lateral projection. Edge detection, line profile analysis, and dedicated radial head ROI analysis all confirm smooth, continuous cortical margins without focal irregularities.
impression: No radiographic evidence of acute fracture, dislocation, or other gross abnormality on this lateral elbow radiograph. Normal fat pad signs. Intact cortical margins throughout the visualized distal humerus, radial head, olecranon, and proximal forearm bones. This assessment is based on a single lateral view with normal fat pad signs, which provides high negative predictive value for occult elbow fracture.
limitations: 1) Image is an 8-bit PNG conversion from an unknown original (likely 12-16 bit DICOM), resulting in irreversible loss of dynamic range and all DICOM metadata (patient ID, laterality, acquisition parameters, kVp, mAs). 2) Single lateral view only — an anteroposterior (AP) view and oblique projection are needed for complete elbow assessment. Radial head fractures, medial/lateral epicondyle fractures, and varus/valgus alignment abnormalities may be invisible on lateral-only imaging. 3) Anatomical content occupies only approximately 45% of the original image width, with the left portion being empty background, reducing effective spatial resolution. 4) The wrist and distal carpal bones are incompletely visualized. 5) Laterality (right vs. left elbow) cannot be determined from the image alone. 6) Patient age is unknown; if this is a pediatric patient, physeal (growth plate) assessment takes on greater clinical significance. 7) Derived images (CLAHE, edge detection, window/level) are supporting visualizations only — no finding on a processed image was accepted without confirmation on the original. 8) No clinical context (mechanism of injury, tenderness location, patient age) was available to guide interpretation. A negative radiographic finding does not exclude occult fracture in the setting of high clinical suspicion.

findings: Lateral/oblique radiograph of a pediatric upper extremity showing a both-bone mid-diaphyseal forearm fracture involving both the radius and ulna at approximately the same longitudinal level. The ulnar fracture demonstrates a transverse to slightly oblique fracture line with visible cortical disruption and mild step-off. The radial fracture at a similar level shows cortical disruption with possible bowing component. Displacement and angulation are present but cannot be precisely quantified from this single non-standard projection. No obvious comminution or butterfly fragments are visible. Growth plates (physes) are open at the distal radius and distal ulna, confirming skeletal immaturity; estimated skeletal age approximately 6-13 years. The fracture is extra-physiolastic with no extension into the distal growth plates. The elbow joint appears grossly congruent. Mild soft tissue swelling is present around the fracture zone. Hand morphology shows abnormalities including apparent syndactyly with fused digits and poorly individualized carpal structures, which may represent congenital deformity. Chronicity is uncertain: some agents identified periosteal reaction and early callus suggesting subacute healing (1-4 weeks), while others found sharp fracture margins with no callus consistent with acute injury. This disagreement could not be resolved through image processing alone.
impression: Both-bone mid-diaphyseal forearm fracture (radius and ulna) in a skeletally immature pediatric patient. The fracture pattern is transverse to short-oblique with mild displacement and angulation. The injury is consistent with direct trauma to the mid-forearm. Association with congenital hand and forearm anomaly (possible radioulnar synostosis with syndactyly) cannot be excluded on this single view and warrants clinical correlation.
limitations: Single non-standard oblique/lateral projection severely limits assessment. True displacement magnitude, rotational malalignment, comminution, and anterior-posterior angulation cannot be quantified without an orthogonal AP view. The clenched hand position prevents adequate evaluation of the carpal bones, metacarpals, and individual phalanges for associated fractures. The distal radioulnar joint cannot be properly assessed. Fracture chronicity (acute vs subacute) remains unresolved due to conflicting agent assessments and inherent image quality limitations. Soft tissue compartment syndrome risk cannot be assessed radiographically. No contralateral comparison view is available. All agent analyses used the same model (qwen3.6-27b); agreement between agents reflects consistency of independent runs rather than cross-model validation.

findings: Lateral projection of the distal tibia/fibula, ankle, and foot (heel left, forefoot right; no side marker; no physical scale). Congruent tibiotalar joint with preserved, uniform joint space; smooth continuous talar dome and tibial plafond without cortical step-off; posterior subtalar joint space appears preserved. No displaced fracture, no dislocation, and no hardware. No fracture line meeting the council's standing criteria (traceable in the original, cutting across trabecular flow, endpoints at cortex, persisting across two independent edge methods) was identified in the hindfoot, midfoot, or in-field forefoot; the straight right-edge collimation boundary was explicitly rejected as a classic fracture-line mimic. The posterior calcaneal cortex is smooth, continuous, and rounded; no posteroinferior calcaneal spur is present and no Achilles-insertion calcification is seen (the posteroinferior spur raised by a single agent in first pass was not confirmed on enhanced re-review and was reclassified as artifact/mislocalization by its originator). A small beak at the posterosuperior Achilles enthesis was reported by one agent as a normal variant/mild enthesophyte with a faint original counterpart, but was not corroborated by the other reviewers (possible variant, uncertain). A focal 'mottled lucency' of the talar body reported by one agent in first pass was adjudicated by four independent reviews as superimposition of the talar neck over the body plus film grain, not a true focal lesion. Soft tissues show a smooth contour without focal swelling; the heel pad is thin and uniform (~10-15 px at standardized stations); the Achilles tendon appears continuous. Quantitative geometry: the foot is in ~25-30 degrees of plantarflexion concentrated at the talus/forefoot (metatarsal axis ~24.5 deg below horizontal; tibiometatarsal ~60 deg vs normal 10-25), the calcaneal pitch is normal (22.7 deg), and Bohler's angle is ~56 deg (normal 20-40) - elevated beyond the ~5-8 deg landmark error band by two independent reviewers, indicating intrinsic cavus-type calcaneal geometry. The fibula projects ~18 px from the tibia, confirming the view is rotated off true lateral, so all angles carry projection bias.
impression: Lateral ankle/foot radiograph in a plantarflexed (equinus-type), rotated off-true-lateral position: congruent ankle and subtalar joints, no fracture or dislocation demonstrable above this image's detection limit, no soft-tissue swelling, and no calcaneal spur; Bohler's angle (~56 deg) is abnormally elevated for a non-intrinsic cause and suggests cavus-type calcaneal geometry (e.g., positional/deformity-related or old change) that requires a true-lateral view for confirmation. Overall: no acute osseous injury identified on this single oblique film; the dominant measurable abnormality is the plantarflexed, rotated foot position with elevated calcaneal pitch geometry.
limitations: Single oblique (not true lateral) projection: the ~18 px fibula-tibia separation biases every angular measurement (~5-8 deg landmark/projection error band); a true-lateral repeat is needed to confirm the elevated Bohler angle and its etiology, and no AP/oblique/weight-bearing views are available. The toes and distal phalanges are truncated by the right-edge crop and cannot be assessed. Low-resolution 373x454 px film scan with no physical scale (linear measurements are pixel-based only) and no side marker or clinical metadata. Practical detection limit ~17 px line length / ~4 grey-level contrast, so sub-millimetre hairline fractures, a very small calcaneal enthesophyte, and a very small talar lesion cannot be excluded. Film grain and background gradient (sigma ~1.2 grey levels) limit contrast; enhancement artifacts (CLAHE speckle, edge halos, denoising swirls, contour slippage onto the beam-field edge) were documented and guarded against, and derived images are supporting visualizations only. All six analysis agents were independent instances of the same model (qwen3.8-27b), so cross-agent agreement indicates consistency between runs, not independent cross-model validation. Unresolved: etiology of the elevated Bohler angle, exact degree and direction of foot rotation, presence of a possible small Achilles-enthesis beak, and bone mineralization (not assessable on a single rescanned lateral).

findings: Single oblique/rotated AP-type radiograph of one forearm, distal humerus to proximal carpus, in a skeletally immature child (open distal radial physis, ossified capitellum and radial head, olecranon apophyseal ossification center, ~3 carpal ossification centers); laterality indeterminate (no R/L marker); field truncated at the proximal carpal row. Elbow: joints congruent, radiocapitellar line congruent (~4 px offset); a thin smooth lucent line (full-image ~945-995 x, 252-270 y) above a small rounded, well-corticated, axially aligned olecranon-tip ossification center - present at 1:1 native resolution with dense parallel margins and a narrow mid-band intensity dip matching the in-image normal distal radial physis control, no displacement, no true cortical notch (a notched impression at 4x zoom is a resampling artifact), no periosteal reaction and no convincing soft-tissue swelling: read as the normal olecranon apophyseal physis. Distal ulna: an oblique lucent cleft (full-image ~830-870 x, 1130-1175 y) with a small separate low-density fragment (~5x4 mm) laterally offset from the ulnar axis - bone assignment by continuity tracing from the carpal-articulation anchor (3 of 4 tracing agents; the distal radius is the wide bone with the transverse physis and carpal-articulating epiphysis). The cleft lacks the narrow dip-with-dense-sclerotic-margins signature shown by the normal radial physis in the same image, runs obliquely, and carries an irregular fragment; with only ~3 carpal centers (skeletal age ~3-6 y) an ossified distal ulnar epiphysis of this size is atypical. Findings favor a nondisplaced distal ulnar physeal/metaphyseal (styloid) fracture; a normal/variant distal ulnar ossification center is the main alternative and is not excluded on this projection. Distal radius is normal (smooth transverse open physis, no injury). Mid-forearm: radial and ulnar diaphyseal cortices continuous from the elbow anchors to the wrist; no buckle/hairline fracture and no periosteal reaction; the mid-shaft lucency is the normal wide pediatric medullary canal.
impression: Suspected nondisplaced distal ulnar physeal (metaphyseal/styloid) fracture with a small fragment, on a single truncated oblique view - the principal alternative (normal variant of distal ulnar ossification) cannot be excluded in-image. The olecranon lucent line is a normal apophyseal physis (not an avulsion on imaging). No other fracture or dislocation identified; elbow and forearm shafts are intact. Recommend dedicated non-truncated wrist PA and true lateral radiographs with clinical correlation (distal ulnar point tenderness/DRUJ exam) to confirm or exclude the distal ulnar injury.
limitations: Single oblique/rotated projection: the posterior humeral line is uninterpretable and the elbow was not assessed on a true lateral; no dedicated elbow or wrist views available. Field of view truncated at the proximal carpus (distal carpal row incomplete). Laterality indeterminate (no marker on image). The distal ulna superimposes the radial epiphysis in projection at the level of the cleft, and the perpendicular intensity profiles of the cleft extend beyond the small distal fragment into lucent space, so both geometric/partial-volume confounds temper the fracture read. One of four tracing agents assigned the cleft to the distal radius (council consensus: ulna, by the carpal-articulation anchor). All six council agents are independent runs of the same model (qwen3.8-27b): agreement reflects consistency, not cross-model validation. A nondisplaced olecranon avulsion and a very faint periosteal line at the image margins cannot be formally excluded; clinical correlation is required.

findings: Single oblique radiograph of a pediatric upper limb (elbow flexed ~90 degrees, hand in semi-fist; laterality indeterminable). Mid-forearm: focal transverse lucent line with a small cortical step/kink at the mid-diaphysis (image coordinates x ~0.50-0.57, y ~0.37-0.41), with mild angulation of the wider bone and a fainter companion transverse line in the other bone; the feature is present in the unmodified original and is corroborated by native-resolution crops, edge mapping and intensity profiles (focal dip of ~30 gray units at x ~680 px on focal-minus-control subtraction; apparent image-plane angulation 5-11 degrees with high fit sensitivity). Skeletally immature: open smooth physes at distal humerus and distal radius, 4-5 small rounded carpal ossification centers, multiple elbow ossification centers; distal radial physis smooth and continuous (physeal injury screen negative). No definite fracture, dislocation or physeal injury at the elbow, wrist or visible hand; central metacarpal/carpal confluence is partially non-assessable due to fist superimposition (1.7% pixel saturation at fist center; 0% at the lesion level). No soft-tissue swelling, gas or foreign body. Two additional long bones with cortical and medullary morphology (a second superimposed limb, most consistent with a contralateral forearm) run obliquely behind the carpal cluster in the lower right; a bright band at the right edge is consistent with the torso; fine wavy external texture is present at the bottom-right corner (non-anatomic). All measurements are in pixel or image-plane units; no physical scale is present in the image.
impression: Findings most consistent with a non-displaced or subtly displaced mid-forearm diaphyseal fracture (acute vs healing not distinguishable on this single oblique view) in a pediatric patient, with a second superimposed limb (contralateral forearm) in the lower right; no other definite acute abnormality at the elbow, wrist or visible hand; confirm and localize with a standard AP/lateral pair when clinically indicated.
limitations: Single non-standard oblique projection without an orthogonal pair; laterality undetermined; no physical scale (all values in pixels/degrees); 8-bit PNG without DICOM metadata; central metacarpal/carpal detail partially unrecoverable due to superimposition and local saturation; second-limb superimposition limits assessment of the ulnar hand and its exact orientation/level is undetermined; one reviewer found no cortical step (mild ulnar bowing only), so the characterization and timing of the mid-forearm lesion remain uncertain; a single-agent report of a faint transverse lucency near the distal ulna is unconfirmed; contrast/edge enhancement (CLAHE, unsharp mask, Canny) can exaggerate cortical edges and was not used to assert periosteal reaction.

findings: Lateral view of the ankle and foot. The distal tibia and fibula appear intact without obvious fracture. The ankle joint space is preserved. The talocrural, subtalar, and midtarsal joints appear within normal limits. No significant osteophytic changes or gross bone destruction are noted in the visualized portions of the calcaneus or tarsal bones.
impression: No acute fracture or dislocation identified in the visualized ankle and foot.
limitations: Single lateral view provided; limited evaluation of the medial and anterior structures. Image contrast is somewhat low.

findings: Lateral view of the forearm and elbow shows a fracture of the proximal radius, specifically involving the radial head. The alignment of the elbow joint appears preserved, but the cortical continuity of the radial head is disrupted. No obvious fracture of the ulna or distal radius/ulna is visualized in this view.
impression: Proximal radial fracture (radial head fracture).
limitations: Single lateral view provided. Clinical correlation and additional views (e.g., AP) are necessary for full assessment of joint stability and alignment.

findings: Complete, displaced fracture of the mid-diaphysis of the radius. The fracture line is clearly visible in the original and sharpened images. There is significant lateral displacement and angulation of the distal fragment.
impression: Displaced mid-shaft radial fracture. Clinical correlation and orthopedic consultation are advised.
limitations: Single view provided; additional views (e.g., AP/lateral) are necessary for full assessment of displacement and potential ulnar involvement.

findings: Lateral radiograph of the foot and ankle. The distal tibia, distal fibula, talus, calcaneus, and remaining tarsal bones demonstrate intact cortical margins without evidence of fracture or dislocation. The tibiotalar joint, subtalar joint, and midfoot articulations appear congruent with preserved joint spaces. No focal bony lucencies, sclerotic lesions, or periosteal reaction identified. Soft tissue outlines are within normal limits without evidence of significant swelling or foreign body. The metatarsals and proximal phalanges appear intact.
impression: No acute osseous abnormality identified on this lateral foot and ankle radiograph. Overall appearance is unremarkable.
limitations: Single lateral view only; AP and oblique views are needed for complete evaluation. Image quality and resolution may limit detection of nondisplaced fractures. This analysis was performed using automated image processing for visualization enhancement and should not replace interpretation by a qualified radiologist.

findings: Lateral X-ray view of the elbow and forearm demonstrating the distal humerus, elbow joint, proximal radius and ulna, and the diaphyses of the radius and ulna. The distal humerus shows normal trabecular pattern and cortical margins. The humeroulnar and humeroradial joint spaces are maintained with congruent articulation. The olecranon and coronoid processes of the ulna appear intact. The radial head and neck are anatomically aligned within the proximal radioulnar joint. The diaphyses of the radius and ulna demonstrate intact cortices with no visible fracture lines. No periosteal reaction, lytic or sclerotic lesions, or joint effusion is identified. Proximal carpal bones are partially visualized at the inferior margin.
impression: Normal lateral radiograph of the elbow and forearm with no acute osseous abnormality identified. No fracture, dislocation, or suspicious osseous lesion is seen in the visualized structures.
limitations: Single lateral view limits assessment of the carrying angle, anterior-posterior alignment, and complete evaluation of the joint spaces. The wrist joint is only partially visualized. Soft tissue evaluation on plain radiograph is limited. Digital image enhancement may introduce artifacts not present in the original acquisition. This is an AI-assisted analysis and does not replace formal radiologist interpretation.

findings: Lateral oblique view of a pediatric left upper extremity (elbow to hand) in a flexed 'fist-to-elbow' position. Bilateral forearm shaft fractures are present in the mid-diaphyseal region of both the radius and ulna. The ulnar fracture demonstrates a buckle (torus) deformity with cortical bulging. The radial fracture shows a transverse oblique fracture line with mild angulation, consistent with a greenstick fracture pattern. No displacement is definitively identified on this single view, though mild angulation is present at the radial fracture site. The distal humeral physis, proximal radioulnar joint, and elbow joint appear intact. The distal radial and ulnar physes are open, consistent with a skeletally immature patient. Carpal bones, metacarpals, and phalanges are intact without fracture. Soft tissue swelling is noted in the mid-forearm region surrounding the fracture zone. Partial thoracic cage is incidentally visualized medially.
impression: Bilateral mid-shaft forearm fractures (both-bone forearm fracture) in a pediatric patient, involving a torus/buckle fracture of the ulna and a greenstick fracture of the radius. This injury pattern is classically associated with a fall on an outstretched hand in children.
limitations: Single lateral oblique view limits full assessment of fracture displacement, rotational deformity, and exact angulation. A true anteroposterior view would be needed for complete evaluation and treatment planning. Pediatric image quality limits fine cortical detail. No clinical history or mechanism of injury is available. Image post-processing (sharpening, contrast enhancement, edge detection) may introduce artifacts and should not be considered as primary diagnostic evidence.

findings: Lateral radiograph of the foot and ankle. A small (few-mm), well-corticated bony spur projects anteroinferiorly from the plantar surface of the calcaneal tuberosity, at the origin of the plantar fascia, consistent with enthesopathy at that site. No fracture line, dislocation, or subluxation is identified in the calcaneus, talus, distal tibia/fibula, midfoot, or visualized metatarsals. The tibiotalar, subtalar, and talonavicular joint spaces appear preserved without definite narrowing. Trabecular bone pattern and cortical outlines are intact; no lytic or sclerotic lesion or periosteal reaction is seen. The longitudinal arch appears mildly low with slight plantar tilting of the talus on this non-weight-bearing film (approximate posterior tibial angle 80 deg, measured; reference values apply to weight-bearing positioning). Soft tissues of the heel and plantar surface are unremarkable; no soft-tissue mass or plantar fascia calcification is identified. The distal forefoot and toes are partially outside the field of view.
impression: Lateral foot/ankle radiograph showing a small plantar calcaneal spur at the plantar fascia origin, consistent with calcaneal enthesopathy; no fracture or joint abnormality is identified. Mild low-arch tendency noted, but arch assessment is not standardized on this non-weight-bearing view. Differential for the spur includes degenerative enthesopathy associated with plantar heel pain; correlation with weight-bearing imaging and clinical findings is recommended.
limitations: Single lateral projection; no AP, oblique, or MIP views, and the distal metatarsals/toes are partially cut off at the image edge. Positioning appears non-weight-bearing (supine/seated), so arch angles are not comparable to weight-bearing reference values. Film-type contrast with limited dynamic range; subtle findings such as a small plantar spur were only appreciable with contrast enhancement and magnification, and hairline fractures or small osteophytes cannot be excluded. Image-processing steps (CLAHE, unsharp masking, edge detection, gamma correction, zoom) were used for visualization only and may introduce artifacts; no 3D data are available. This analysis is a second-opinion support tool and does not replace formal radiologist interpretation or clinical correlation.

findings: Lateral radiograph of the upper extremity including the distal humerus, elbow joint, both forearm bones (radius and ulna) in full, and a partial view of the distal forearm and wrist. Skeletal immaturity is present (visible unfused physes at the distal radius, distal ulna and distal humerus), consistent with a child or adolescent. Cortices of the radius and ulna are continuous over their entire visualized length and alignment of the forearm bones is maintained; no definite displaced fracture, periosteal reaction, or dislocation is identified. At the elbow, a prominent pointed bony projection is seen at the olecranon with an adjacent smaller pointed fragment; this may represent a normal variant or olecranon ossification center but cannot be definitively characterized on a single view. The radial head articulates congruently with the capitellum and the olecranon with the trochlea. The partially visualized wrist shows no definite acute abnormality within the field. No definite soft-tissue swelling, lucent soft-tissue gas, or radiopaque foreign body is identified on the original or contrast-enhanced views.
impression: No definite acute fracture or dislocation identified on this single lateral view of the elbow and forearm in a skeletally immature patient. The prominent pointed olecranon projection with adjacent fragment most likely represents a normal variant or olecranon ossification center in a growing skeleton, although an acute olecranon avulsion lesion cannot be fully excluded without a second view or prior comparison. If clinically indicated, standard two-view (AP and lateral) imaging and correlation with the mechanism and physical examination are recommended.
limitations: Single lateral projection only; no AP view to assess rotation or lateral alignment. Proximal humerus and most of the hand are not included, so those regions cannot be evaluated. The provided file is a cropped grayscale PNG rather than the original DICOM image. Post-processing (grayscale conversion, CLAHE contrast enhancement, unsharp sharpening, Sobel edge enhancement, zoomed crops, bone/soft-tissue windows) was used for visualization only and may exaggerate subtle lucent lines; no finding was made solely on an enhanced image. Skeletal immaturity means normal physeal lucencies can mimic pathology; findings require clinical correlation.

findings: Frontal projection of an upper limb with the elbow flexed and the hand in a clenched fist, including the distal humerus, elbow, radius, ulna, wrist and hand. No definite displaced fracture, dislocation or joint-space abnormality is seen at the elbow, distal humerus or wrist. In the mid-diaphysis of the ulna there is a faint transverse lucent line with a subtle cortical notch; at a similar level there is a focal cortical irregularity/thickening of the mid-diaphysis of the radius. These subtle mid-forearm findings could represent a subtle/non-displaced both-bone (radius and ulna) forearm fracture, or could be normal variants (e.g. nutrient foramina) or projectional artifacts. The carpal and metacarpal bones are difficult to fully assess because of the clenched, superimposed fist, although no obvious fracture is identified.
impression: No definite displaced fracture or dislocation is seen. Subtle mid-forearm cortical irregularities are present (faint transverse lucent line in the ulna mid-shaft and focal cortical thickening in the radius mid-shaft at a similar level); a subtle or non-displaced both-bone forearm fracture cannot be excluded. If there is local tenderness or a history of trauma, dedicated AP and lateral forearm radiographs and comparison with prior films, if available, are recommended. If the patient is clinically normal, these findings may represent normal variants.
limitations: Single, non-standard projection (not a dedicated two-view forearm film). The hand is clenched/flexed, limiting assessment of the carpal, metacarpal and phalangeal bones. The mid-forearm findings are subtle and of uncertain significance (cannot be distinguished from nutrient foramina, normal variants, or projectional artifacts). The image is a PNG with fixed windowing, which may limit detection of subtle changes. No prior images are available for comparison and the clinical context (acute trauma vs chronic) is unknown. Findings should be correlated clinically.

findings: The cardiac silhouette is enlarged, consistent with cardiomegaly. Bilateral opacities are present in the lower lung zones, which, combined with the blunting of the costophrenic angles, are highly suggestive of bilateral pleural effusions. There are also signs of pulmonary congestion/infiltration. Multiple medical lines and monitoring leads are overlying the chest.
impression: Cardiomegaly with bilateral pleural effusions and pulmonary congestion.
limitations: Portable AP projection may exaggerate cardiac size. Overlying monitoring hardware and suboptimal inspiratory effort may limit detailed evaluation of lung parenchyma.

findings: The lung fields appear relatively clear without obvious consolidation, large masses, or significant pleural effusion. The cardiac silhouette is within normal limits. No definite evidence of pneumothorax or acute bony fracture is visualized.
impression: Normal chest radiograph.
limitations: Single AP/PA view. Suboptimal inspiration may slightly affect cardiac silhouette assessment. Model outputs suggested potential infiltration and fibrosis, but these were not clearly identifiable on visual inspection of the original image.

findings: A prominent medical device, likely a central venous catheter, is visible with its tip in the superior vena cava/right atrium region. There is an area of increased opacity in the right mid-to-lower lung field, which may represent a mass or nodule, as supported by model predictions (Nodule: 0.70, Mass: 0.65). The mediastinum appears widened (Enlarged Cardiomediastinum: 0.51), though specific cardiomegaly was not strongly indicated. Overlying breast tissue limits the evaluation of the lung bases.
impression: Right mid-to-lower lung opacity suspicious for a mass or nodule, with a central venous catheter in situ and widened mediastinum.
limitations: Overlying soft tissue (breast shadows) obscures the lung bases. Image projection (AP vs PA) affects cardiac and mediastinal silhouette assessment.

findings: Bilateral patchy opacities are present, more prominent in the mid-to-lower lung zones. Multiple external monitoring leads are visible. Possible pleural effusions at the costophrenic angles.
impression: Bilateral pulmonary opacities, differential includes pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or pulmonary hemorrhage.
limitations: Portable AP projection limits cardiac silhouette assessment. Significant overlying ECG leads may obscure lung details. Image quality is limited by portable technique.

findings: The lung fields appear clear without obvious consolidation or pleural effusion. Heart size is within normal limits. Bony structures and soft tissues appear unremarkable. Large breast shadows are noted.
impression: Normal chest radiograph.
limitations: Large breast shadows may partially obscure the lung bases.

findings: Possible bilateral atelectasis and pleural effusion, more pronounced in the lower lung zones. Mediastinum appears widened, though this may be due to the AP projection. Lung markings in the bases are somewhat obscured.
impression: Bilateral lower zone atelectasis and possible pleural effusions.
limitations: AP projection complicates assessment of cardiomegaly and mediastinal width. Significant overlying soft tissue and external leads may obscure detail.

findings: There is a prominent opacity in the right lung field, particularly in the middle and lower zones. A medical device, appearing to be a pleural drain or chest tube, is visible on the right side. Lung markings and structures are partially obscured by the opacity and the device.
impression: Right-sided lung opacity with an indwelling pleural drain.
limitations: Presence of medical devices and potential patient positioning issues may obscure fine details. Single view limitation.

findings: Dense opacification is present at the right lung base, obscuring the right costophrenic angle and hemidiaphragm. This is consistent with a large right-sided pleural effusion. Associated features may include atelectasis or consolidation in the underlying lung parenchyma.
impression: Large right-sided pleural effusion.
limitations: The dense opacification obscures the lower lung zones and diaphragm, making it difficult to definitively distinguish between pleural fluid and parenchymal consolidation without further imaging or clinical correlation.

findings: Opacification of the left lower lung zone obscuring the left costophrenic angle and diaphragm, consistent with pleural effusion. There is also evidence of underlying atelectasis and potential consolidation in the left base. The cardiomediastinal silhouette appears moderately enlarged.
impression: Left-sided pleural effusion and associated atelectasis/consolidation.
limitations: Single AP view projection. Limited ability to distinguish between effusion and consolidation without lateral view or clinical correlation. Potential for overlapping structures to mimic enlargement.

Several available pretrained models (xrv DenseNet/ResNet/PSPNet and the xrv view classifier, plus the wrist-fracture YOLOv8 and bone-fracture classifier) behaved out-of-distribution on this image and were excluded; the interpretation rests on direct visual inspection and the MedSAM-verified CT-ratio measurement.

findings: Portable AP (supine/semi-erect) chest radiograph of a monitored patient with low lung volumes. Bilateral hazy parenchymal opacities with basilar predominance: a dense retrocardiac opacity obscuring the left hemidiaphragm and left costophrenic angle (left lower lobe collapse and/or consolidation and/or effusion), and a hazy, obscured right base with loss of the right costophrenic angle. Cardiac silhouette appears enlarged, likely exaggerated by AP/supine projection. Trachea midline; no mediastinal shift. No pneumothorax; no fracture identified. Devices: multiple ECG monitoring electrodes, external IV lines, a thin line running from the left neck into the mediastinum (possible catheter), and a looped (hairpin-coiled) tubular structure with a small round radiodense focus over the left clavicle/first rib - a coiled catheter or external tubing, not definitively characterizable on a single frontal view. Dental restoration in the mandible (incidental).
impression: Bilateral pleural effusions with basilar atelectasis/consolidation, including a dense retrocardiac (left lower lobe) opacity, in a monitored patient; apparent cardiomegaly likely projectional. Findings are most consistent with fluid-overload/immobility-related changes in a critically ill patient. No pneumothorax or fracture. The looped left-infraclavicular device (catheter vs external tubing) requires clinical correlation.
limitations: Single portable AP supine view; no lateral view and no prior for comparison. Supine/AP technique magnifies the cardiac silhouette, allows free pleural fluid to layer posteriorly (extent not measurable), and causes basilar vascular crowding that can mimic edema. Multiple external devices (ECG electrodes, IV lines, looped left-infraclavicular tubing) overlie the lung fields; the looped device cannot be definitively characterized (indwelling catheter vs external tubing) without clinical correlation. AI model limitations: the supervised models disagreed in degree (DenseNet more positive than ResNet50); the segmentation models under-segmented the heart and over-segmented the diaphragm/scapulae, so a quantitative cardiothoracic ratio is unreliable; zero-shot vision-language scores are uncalibrated. Interpretation relies on the original image, with model outputs used only as supporting evidence.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (likely AP/portable) with four ECG electrodes and external monitoring cables overlying the chest; no indwelling central line, NG tube or chest tube is identified. Diffuse bilateral patchy airspace opacities are present in all lung zones, confluent in the left lower zone with partial silhouetting of the left hemidiaphragm and left heart border. Zone quantification (PSPNet lung masks) confirms increased density in every zone of both lungs (apical mean intensities ~89-92), with the left mid and lower zones clearly denser than the right (left lower mean 101 vs right lower 81; fraction of hyperdense pixels 41% vs 30%). A vague, ill-defined density in the right mid zone is part of the diffuse patchy process and does not correspond to a discrete nodule (ROI max intensity 115). No pneumothorax is seen. The left costophrenic angle is obscured and a small left pleural effusion cannot be excluded. The cardiomediastinal silhouette is prominent, most likely magnification from the AP projection; classifier scores argue against true cardiomegaly. No rib fractures or other acute bony abnormality.
impression: Multifocal bilateral airspace disease with left basal predominance, most consistent with multifocal pneumonia; asymmetric pulmonary edema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic) cannot be excluded on a single frontal view.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral or prior comparison; no DICOM metadata, so projection, patient factors and timing are unknown and AP/portable acquisition is inferred from the monitoring equipment, which also magnifies the cardiac silhouette. 8-bit PNG with moderate noise and a black band at the inferior edge. ECG electrodes and cables overlying the chest can mimic or obscure focal findings. Model outputs are supporting only: two in-domain chest X-ray classifiers were validated on this image with inverted-image negative controls (one content-insensitive classifier was rejected and not used for any finding), one vision-language model was used as a ranking only, and pneumonia versus edema cannot be separated definitively without clinical context.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph of a critically ill patient with multiple support devices (ECG leads, central venous catheter, an enteric tube coursing down the midline, and a radiopaque marker/label on the left). There is diffuse bilateral hazy alveolar and interstitial opacity with basilar predominance. The opacification is asymmetric, with greater density in the left mid and lower zones than the right (the right mid-zone is comparatively more aerated). Both costophrenic angles are obscured by basilar opacity, consistent with pleural effusion and/or basilar atelectasis/consolidation. No definite pneumothorax and no discrete, well-circumscribed mass are identified. The cardiac silhouette is not reliably assessable.
impression: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacification, most consistent with pulmonary edema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic/ARDS) in a critically ill, supported patient, with superimposed bilateral pleural effusions and a left-predominant focal consolidation/atelectasis component.
limitations: Single 8-bit PNG of a portable AP film (not the original DICOM), with patient rotation and multiple superimposed support devices that obscure and can mimic pathology. The AP projection magnifies the cardiac silhouette, so cardiomegaly could not be reliably assessed. Pretrained models (DenseNet, ResNet, PSPNet, BiomedCLIP, MedSAM) were trained predominantly on cleaner PA films and gave divergent, partly out-of-distribution outputs; their outputs were used only as supporting evidence, and any single model score was not allowed to drive a finding. No lateral view or comparison films were available. The exact positions of the tube/line tips and the identity of the 'GJ' marker/radiopaque object are not fully characterized.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph. A large, dense, homogeneous opacity in the left mid-to-lower zone obscuring the left hemidiaphragm, the left costophrenic angle, and part of the left heart border, with a superior border in the mid-zone and no definite air bronchograms; the left upper zone remains aerated. Increased interstitial/patchy opacity in the right mid-to-lower lung. A radiopaque airway tube in the cervical trachea (endotracheal or tracheostomy tube) with an adjacent midline line. Multiple external ECG electrodes. A coiled tubular device in the right lower zone and a midline tubular line (feeding tube or central venous catheter). The trachea is midline without definite mediastinal shift. No definite pneumothorax; no definite rib fracture identified.
impression: Large left basilar opacity, most consistent with a large left pleural effusion +/- left lower lobe atelectasis/consolidation, with lesser right basilar opacity (possible edema or infiltrate), in a patient with multiple support devices.
limitations: Single portable AP view (magnification and suboptimal penetration), patient rotation, and superimposed external devices limit assessment. A single frontal view cannot reliably distinguish effusion from consolidation from atelectasis, exclude mediastinal shift, or fully assess the cardiac silhouette. Pretrained model outputs (xrv DenseNet/ResNet, BiomedCLIP) are approximate, partly uncertain on this degraded image, and do not substitute for clinical correlation. A lateral view and/or thoracic ultrasound would better characterize the left opacity and the airway/line devices.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph of an adult with bilateral breast shadows. (1) Right-sided implantable infusion port in the right mid chest wall (projected over the right mid lung zone, about the 4th-6th rib level): flat low-density body with two lateral suture-tab wings, each with a round hole, and a radiopaque catheter that ascends over the right lung, forms a mild loop (excess length) at the right apex, and descends along the right mediastinum; the distal tip is projected over the lower SVC/cavoatrial region but its exact position is not determinable against the cardiac silhouette. (2) A cluster of about 7 small (2-4 mm) ovoid/teardrop dense objects with dense rims and relatively lucent centers in the right mid-lower lung zone just above the right hemidiaphragm; in this 8-bit image their peak density is below bone level, so the differential includes small surgical clips (prior procedure), calcified lymph nodes/granulomas, vessels or airways on end, or small foreign bodies. (3) A hazy rounded soft-tissue opacity of about 2-2.5 cm in the left mid lung zone, abutting the left heart border, with aerated lung lateral to it; differential includes a pulmonary nodule or mass, confluent pulmonary vessels, or a pericardial/epicardial border structure. (4) A few small (2-8 mm) dense ring-like and dot-like objects near the left heart border/hilum and in the right mid lung zone. (5) No pneumothorax (apices and lateral pleura clear on lung window), no pleural effusion (both costophrenic angles sharp), no focal consolidation. (6) Cardiomediastinal silhouette normal in size (cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.29 by image analysis). (7) Osseous structures intact, no acute fracture; the straight linear bands over the left heart border are rib crossings. (8) Gastric bubble present; no pneumoperitoneum seen.
impression: Single frontal chest radiograph without acute cardiopulmonary process. The main abnormality is a rounded 2-2.5 cm soft-tissue opacity in the left mid lung zone (pulmonary nodule/mass until characterized by lateral view or CT). Additionally: right-sided port-a-cath with catheter loop at the right apex and tip in the lower SVC region, and a cluster of about 7 small dense ovoid objects in the right mid-lower lung zone (most likely small surgical clips or calcified nodes).
limitations: Single frontal view (no lateral) and no prior images for comparison. 8-bit PNG without DICOM metadata: compressed dynamic range (bone peaks around 211/250), so thin metallic objects cannot be reliably distinguished from dense calcification and no absolute HU quantification is possible. The catheter tip is not clearly visible against the cardiac silhouette. Breast shadows overlie the lower lung zones, reducing sensitivity for basilar disease. The cardiothoracic ratio was estimated by image analysis (0.29), with the heart mask of the segmentation model under-segmented and discarded. The exact nature of the clustered ovoid objects and of the left mid-zone opacity cannot be determined on a single frontal film. Pretrained model outputs (in-domain chest classifiers and zero-shot vision-language model) were used only as supporting evidence after sanity checks; out-of-domain models (pediatric wrist detector, community bone-fracture classifier) were run and rejected as untrustworthy. CT of the chest is recommended to characterize the left mid-zone opacity and the right mid-lower cluster.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. Large, well-circumscribed, rounded to lobulated soft-tissue mass in the left upper zone, projecting over the aortic arch and left hilum, with smooth convex margins; the main component measures 202x148 px (area ~22800 px^2 at 1024 px image size) and is soft-tissue dense (mean intensity 118 vs 91 in the contralateral aerated control). Structure segmentation places most of the mass within the left lung territory, with its inferior part fusing with the left heart border; the left heart border is therefore partly obscured and cardiac silhouette assessment is limited. The right lung is well aerated and clear; no definite consolidation, pleural effusion or pneumothorax. The trachea is essentially midline (no significant deviation). An irregular, mottled dense structure is projected over the right paratracheal neck (possible foreign body, calcification or external artifact; indeterminate). A faint indeterminate punctate density is present near the left mid-axillary line (likely a vessel in cross-section or minor artifact; no clinical weight). No objective evidence of an elevated fissure or lobar collapse on this view. An 'R' orientation marker and alphanumeric overlay are present in the upper left corner.
impression: Large well-circumscribed left upper zone / juxtahilar mass (intrapulmonary or paratracheal-hilar), most likely a neoplastic lesion (lymphoma if the patient is young, primary lung neoplasm if adult) or a congenital/cystic lesion (bronchogenic cyst, congenital pulmonary airway malformation); no acute parenchymal process otherwise identified. Patient habitus appears young but age could not be reliably determined from this image.
limitations: Single frontal view only; without a lateral view the mass cannot be definitively localised as intrapulmonary versus mediastinal. Patient age/sex cannot be reliably determined (visual impression suggests a young patient; zero-shot CLIP habitus prompts weakly suggest adult; no demographic model was used). Cardiac size is unassessable where the mass overlaps the left heart border. Lower lung zones are partly obscured by overlying soft tissue. No scale marker, so all sizes are in pixels. Classifier scores (DenseNet-121/224, ResNet-50/512) are calibrated operating points trained on adult cohorts and were used only as supporting evidence; PSPNet segmentation is coarse and under-calls hilar/aortic labels; MedSAM output is a prompt-dependent geometric measurement. Out-of-domain models (wrist YOLO, bone-fracture classifier) were run as negative controls and excluded as untrustworthy.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. Diffuse bilateral reticulonodular/interstitial-alveolar opacities involving all lung zones, most pronounced in the mid and lower zones. Dense confluent opacity at the left base partially obscuring the left hemidiaphragm and the left heart border. Cardiac silhouette indeterminate due to overlying opacities, with borderline enlargement by model scores. No pneumothorax. No large pleural effusion; a small left basilar effusion cannot be excluded. No definite rib fracture or other acute skeletal abnormality. External artifacts: a perforated metallic arch-bar/splint-type device projecting over the mandible and oral cavity, a small ring-shaped metallic object over the right shoulder, and two ECG electrodes over the lateral chest walls. A cluster of approximately 7-8 small ring-shaped metallic densities projects over the right mid-lower lung field (surgical clips or external metallic object; identity not determinable).
impression: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacification consistent with a diffuse parenchymal process (differential: diffuse pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or diffuse metastatic disease including lymphangitic carcinomatosis) with a dominant left lower lobe consolidation component; multiple external metallic and ECG artifacts; no acute skeletal injury identified.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral or prior comparison; hazy image with reduced contrast; cardiac size assessment limited by overlying opacities and projection; multiple external metallic/ECG artifacts; identity of the metallic cluster over the right mid-lower lung field undetermined; pretrained model scores are calibrated operating-point values, not probabilities; the segmentation model's heart mask failed and was excluded from conclusions; out-of-domain models (pediatric-wrist detector, bone-fracture classifier) misfired on this image and were excluded; zero-shot vision-language results are prompt-sensitive.

findings: Frontal (AP, likely portable/supine) chest radiograph, upper-to-mid thorax. Bilateral diffuse hazy pulmonary opacities with a reticular-interstitial and patchy-alveolar component, perihilar and lower-zone predominant, more confluent in the left mid-lower zone; the right lung shows patchy opacities with small lucent foci. Hila are indistinct. The cardiac silhouette appears prominent but cannot be reliably sized (image is cropped and AP magnification is present). Trachea is midline. No pneumothorax, no definite rib or clavicular fracture, and no definite large pleural effusion are identified (the costophrenic angles are not fully included). Multiple external ECG electrodes and monitoring lead wires overlie the chest; a thin linear structure overlying the right lung is most consistent with an external monitoring lead. An 'L' side marker is present.
impression: Abnormal: bilateral diffuse pulmonary opacities. The pattern (bilateral, perihilar and lower-zone/dependent predominant, with indistinct hila) is most consistent with pulmonary edema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic), but multifocal pneumonia or a mixed alveolar process is a close alternative; the specific etiology cannot be determined from this single cropped frontal image.
limitations: Single frontal (AP) projection cropped to the upper-mid thorax: the diaphragm and costophrenic angles are not fully included, so pleural effusion and basilar disease cannot be fully assessed and the cardiac silhouette cannot be sized (AP magnification). External ECG electrodes and monitoring leads overlie the lung fields and can mimic or obscure pathology. The image is an 8-bit (windowed) PNG rather than raw DICOM. Pretrained-model outputs are limited: classifier scores are biased by the cropped field (lower-zone and cardiac-silhouette labels are unreliable) and the models disagree on the specific etiology (edema vs pneumonia); the community bone-fracture model was not relied on (no fracture seen on inspection). Clinical and laboratory correlation is required.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph of an inpatient with multiple ECG electrodes and a left-sided central venous catheter whose tip lies within the mediastinum (likely SVC/RA junction); no endotracheal tube. Diffuse bilateral airspace and interstitial opacities, more extensive on the right, with patchy right mid-lung consolidation and air bronchograms. Dense right base opacity obscures the right hemidiaphragm and right heart border (right lower zone consolidation with probable right pleural effusion). Milder reticular/ground-glass opacities in the left lung with haziness at the left base (possible small left effusion). Zone density quantification confirms right > left predominance (right base mean 152 vs left upper 78). No pneumothorax identified at the apices or chest wall. Trachea midline. No convincing cardiomegaly on this AP projection (heart/thorax width ratio ~0.51; classifier cardiomegaly scores near 0). No definite rib fracture.
impression: Diffuse bilateral airspace disease, right greater than left, with dense right base consolidation/effusion in a critically ill patient. Most consistent with multifocal pneumonia (with parapneumonic effusion) or non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema/ARDS; cardiogenic edema is less likely given the absence of cardiomegaly and low edema scores, but not excluded.
limitations: Single portable supine AP film: cardiac size is magnified, pleural fluid layers posteriorly (underestimating effusion size), and sensitivity for a small pneumothorax is reduced. Overlying ECG electrodes and the catheter obscure parts of the lung fields and the catheter tip is not fully verifiable. No prior studies for comparison. Pretrained model outputs on this inpatient image are only partially reliable (many pathology scores near the neutral operating point), so they were used solely as supporting evidence alongside direct visual inspection. Clinical and laboratory correlation is required to distinguish pneumonia from edema/ARDS.

findings: Frontal (PA, erect) chest radiograph. A large, well-circumscribed round-to-oval structure occupies the left lower hemithorax; its superior border is smooth, convex and sharply marginated, projecting up to approximately the 4th-5th anterior rib level, i.e. about 3 rib levels above the right hemidiaphragm dome (which is normally the higher side by 1-3 rib levels). The interior of the structure is of approximately aerated-lung density (slightly more lucent than adjacent lung on pixel measurement) with visible vascular/reticular markings and overlying ribs; no definite air bronchograms, fat or large air collection within it. A thin hyperlucent (gas-density) crescent runs along its inferior/inferolateral margin, and below that a dense curved band is seen at the left hemidiaphragm level, with the gastric gas bubble beneath it; the left hemidiaphragm is not identifiable as a separate thin line. A dense curved band runs along the lateral aspect of the structure. Right lung clear; left lateral costophrenic angle sharp and aerated (no pleural effusion); no pneumothorax; normal cardiomediastinal silhouette; midline trachea; no rib fracture or foreign body identified. 'L' and 'A' orientation markers are present at the top right corner.
impression: Marked elevation of the left hemidiaphragm as a large, well-defined dome-shaped structure in the left lower hemithorax with aerated contents and gas below; most likely left diaphragmatic eventration or phrenic nerve palsy, or a left diaphragmatic (Bochdalek) hernia containing aerated bowel - not separable on a single frontal view. No other acute intrathoracic abnormality identified.
limitations: Single frontal projection only; no lateral view, so the relationship of the dome to the posterior costophrenic sulcus and the thoracic versus subdiaphragmatic location of its contents cannot be established; CT (or a lateral/contrast study) would be required for a definitive diagnosis. The dome interior has aerated-lung density, so its exact composition (aerated bowel, compressed lung, fluid) cannot be determined on projection radiography. Pretrained pathology classifiers (DenseNet, ResNet) gave low scores for atelectasis/effusion/mass/hernia and did not flag the finding; a community bone-fracture model behaved out-of-domain (flagged a blank image as fractured) and was discarded; view classification, the two anatomy segmentation models and the MedSAM delineation were in-domain and cross-validated. No prior images for comparison; upper abdomen partly cropped. Second-opinion support output; not a substitute for clinical correlation.

findings: Frontal (likely supine AP) chest radiograph of an adult. Large, homogeneous left basal/retrocardiac opacity with a smooth upper border running from the left heart border downward and laterally to the left lateral chest wall; the left hemidiaphragm and the medial left costophrenic angle are obscured and the left costophrenic region is opacified; the gastric bubble is visible below the opacity. No air bronchograms, no air-fluid level and no retrocardiac gas are seen. The left hemidiaphragm appears elevated relative to the right. The right hemidiaphragm is also elevated (supine position/hypoinflation) with a sharp right costophrenic angle and otherwise clear right lung base. The cardiac silhouette is not enlarged (cardiothoracic ratio ~0.24-0.30 measured above the opacity); the apparent cardiac prominence is due to the opacity fusing with the heart border. Trachea is midline and mediastinal contours are otherwise unremarkable. A nasogastric/orogastric tube is in place, crossing the diaphragm with its tip in the gastric region. No pneumothorax, no definite nodule or mass, and no rib or clavicle fracture are identified. External artifacts: dental restorations in the mandible, a metallic clip over the left lateral chest wall, and a faint external line over the right neck.
impression: Large left basal/retrocardiac opacity, most consistent with left lower lobe atelectasis, likely with an associated left pleural effusion; a layering left pleural effusion alone or an elevated left hemidiaphragm with gastric distension cannot be excluded on this single frontal view. No cardiomegaly. Nasogastric tube in appropriate position.
limitations: Single frontal view, likely supine AP: no lateral or decubitus view, so pleural effusion, atelectasis and diaphragmatic elevation cannot be definitively separated; AP projection magnifies the heart and mediastinum. 8-bit PNG export without DICOM metadata (no original windowing, no patient or technique data). Deep-learning outputs (DenseNet-121, ResNet-50, PSPNet, BiomedCLIP, MedSAM) were used only as corroborating evidence after flip/view/modality sanity checks; PSPNet diaphragm/heart classes and MedSAM masks proved unreliable in the presence of the opacity, and the automatic CTR was discarded. Subtle nodule-level findings cannot be excluded in an 8-bit rendering.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (likely portable AP, scapulae overlying the lung fields) with external ECG electrodes and multiple monitoring leads overlying the thorax. A patchy, ill-defined opacity occupies the right mid and lower lung zones, extending to the base; it is heterogeneous with internal aerated lucencies (air-bronchogram-like) and irregular borders, rather than a sharply marginated discrete mass. The right costophrenic angle is at least partly preserved, suggesting at most a trace or small effusion. The cardiomediastinal silhouette is within normal limits for a frontal projection and the trachea is midline. The left lung is comparatively clear. Two or three small metallic surgical clips are present below the left hemidiaphragm in the upper abdomen. A small, indeterminate metallic linear density is seen within the right lower zone opacity (possible tiny surgical clip or foreign body; uncertain). No pneumothorax, no definite rib fracture, and no indwelling chest tube or central venous catheter are identified; all linear structures appear to be external monitoring leads.
impression: Patchy right mid and lower zone consolidation, most consistent with pneumonia of the right middle/lower lobe, in a patient monitored with external ECG leads. A pulmonary mass with surrounding infiltrate is less likely but cannot be excluded on this single view; at most a trace right pleural effusion.
limitations: Single frontal view only, likely portable AP with scapular overlap and cardiac magnification; no lateral, decubitus, or prior comparison films, so effusion size and exact lobar localization are uncertain. Image is a digitized 8-bit PNG with reduced dynamic range. External ECG electrodes and lead wires overlie the right lung field and may mask or mimic pathology. Model-based evidence is supporting only: global non-localizing classifiers (DenseNet-121, ResNet-50, MIMIC-trained JF DenseNet) showed a present opacity with weak-to-moderate pneumonia/consolidation signal and no strong mass or cardiomegaly; a promptable segmenter failed to delineate a discrete mass (negative result); zero-shot BiomedCLIP was non-discriminative; out-of-domain models (pediatric-wrist YOLO and a bone-fracture classifier, the latter giving a strong false 'Fractured' positive) were rejected. The small metallic density in the right opacity is indeterminate.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. Large right basilar opacity with a sharp, nearly horizontal superior margin at mid-thoracic level, homogeneous fluid density (no aerated lung below the margin), extending to the lateral chest wall and obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and right heart border, consistent with a large right pleural effusion with adjacent atelectasis/consolidation. Diffuse reticulonodular, mottled parenchymal opacities in the right upper and mid zones; milder mottling around the left hilum. A chest tube (pleural drain) is in situ in the left hemithorax, running from the left axilla down the lateral chest wall toward the left base. No definite pneumothorax: the thin oblique line in the left upper zone follows the course of the left oblique fissure, with no lucent zone devoid of lung markings. The left lung is otherwise aerated to the base; the left costophrenic angle is sharp; gastric air is seen below the left hemidiaphragm. The trachea appears near midline. An indeterminate corner bracket with two-letter text (a study/hospital label) is present in the top right corner.
impression: Large right pleural effusion with adjacent right basilar atelectasis/consolidation, and bilateral (right-predominant) mottled interstitial/alveolar opacities of indeterminate character; chest tube in situ in the left hemithorax; no definite pneumothorax. Single frontal view; etiologies of the effusion and parenchymal pattern cannot be determined from this image alone.
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral view, no prior comparison). Overpenetration reduces contrast in the lower zones; the right hemidiaphragm and right heart border are obscured, and tracheal/mediastinal position cannot be reliably quantified. The top-right marker is a non-standard label; orientation was inferred from the cardiac apex direction (normal). The character of the mottled opacities (infiltrate vs edema vs fibrosis) is indeterminate without clinical data. Pretrained outputs were supporting evidence only: DenseNet-121 (top score effusion) is concordant with the visual reading; PSPNet segmentation failed its sanity check on this image and was rejected; the zero-shot CLIP ranking (pneumothorax top) conflicted with the visual analysis and was not trusted; the pediatric wrist YOLO detector is out of domain and contributed no clinical information.

findings: Frontal (portable AP) chest radiograph. Extensive streaky subcutaneous emphysema, most marked in the right neck, axilla and lateral chest wall, with lesser involvement of the left lateral chest wall. The right hemithorax shows right lung volume loss (right lung area approximately half that of the left) with a lucent peripheral zone between the right lung and the lateral chest wall and a visible lateral lung margin, consistent with a right pneumothorax. No definite gross mediastinal or tracheal shift (trachea approximately midline). A non-specific hazy opacity is present in the left mid-to-lower lung zone. The right hemidiaphragm appears elevated. External ECG monitoring leads/electrodes are present; no definite chest drain is seen.
impression: Probable right pneumothorax with extensive right-predominant subcutaneous emphysema and right lung volume loss, without definite mediastinal shift (no tension physiology). A non-specific left mid-to-lower zone opacity is also present.
limitations: Portable AP projection with patient rotation and external monitoring devices; overall low contrast. Extensive superimposed subcutaneous emphysema overlaps the right pleural space, making it difficult to definitively separate pleural air (pneumothorax) from chest-wall gas - the pneumothorax is probable but not certain. Single frontal view only; no lateral or decubitus view to confirm pneumothorax or effusion. The left mid-to-lower zone opacity is non-specific without additional views or clinical context. Pretrained pathology models are out of distribution for this abnormal film, and their scores were used only as weak corroboration.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. A hazy, ill-defined opacity is present in the left lower lung zone, denser medially (retrocardiac) and extending toward the left costophrenic angle; it obscures the left hemidiaphragm and the left heart border, and the left costophrenic angle is blunted (right costophrenic angle is sharp). The left lower zone is measurably denser than the contralateral zone (mean 128 vs 83 gray levels). No air bronchograms are identified within the opacity. The right lung is clear and well aerated. No pneumothorax. The trachea is midline and there is no mediastinal shift. Cardiothoracic ratio is approximately 0.44 (manual measurement, 0.42-0.46 accounting for the obscured left heart border), so the cardiac silhouette is not enlarged. No definite rib fracture or other skeletal abnormality is visible on direct inspection. A bright band along the inferior image edge is a table/detector artifact, not a finding.
impression: Left lower zone opacity with blunting of the left costophrenic angle, most consistent with a moderate left pleural effusion, likely with associated left lower lobe atelectasis or consolidation. No radiographic evidence of cardiomegaly, pneumothorax, or rib fracture.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral or decubitus): effusion versus consolidation versus atelectasis cannot be fully separated, and a subtle lateral meniscus cannot be confirmed or excluded. PA versus AP projection is unknown, which affects interpretation of the cardiothoracic ratio (a ratio of 0.44 would read slightly smaller if the view is PA). The left heart border is partially obscured by the opacity, adding +/-15 px uncertainty to the CT ratio. No clinical context (age, sex, symptoms) is available. A table/detector artifact band crosses the bottom of the image. The fracture-detection tools available in this environment are trained on wrist radiographs (out of domain) and were rejected, so skeletal assessment rests on direct visual inspection. Both available chest-structure segmentation models under-segmented the heart on this image, so the CT ratio was measured with manually verified landmarks.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (view classifier: Frontal, probability 0.996). Right pleural drainage catheter (chest tube) in situ: it enters the right hemithorax in the upper zone, its proximal segment is coiled in the right upper lung field, and the catheter descends along the right lateral chest wall with its tip curled at the right base. Moderate right lower-zone opacity with blunting/obscuration of the right costophrenic angle and obscuration of the right hemidiaphragm; the right lower lung zone is markedly denser than the corresponding left zone (zone medians 165 vs 124; see measurements/08_lung_zone_stats.csv) and anatomical segmentation classifies the right base as diaphragm rather than aerated lung. No pneumothorax is visible: pulmonary markings extend to the right chest wall, no pleural line is identified, and peripheral density is not more lucent than the left. Left lung field is clear with a sharp left costophrenic angle. Cardiac silhouette is not enlarged (cardiothoracic ratio 0.28). No rib fracture is identified. No other foreign device is present.
impression: Right-sided pleural drainage catheter in situ with a moderate right basal opacity, most consistent with a pleural effusion (partially drained/residual, with or without dependent atelectasis). No definite pneumothorax and no cardiomegaly.
limitations: Single frontal view only; PA vs AP and upright vs supine position are unknown, which affects assessment of effusion distribution and cardiac size; no lateral view. Image is an 8-bit PNG without original DICOM data (display-dependent contrast, no HU). The indwelling tube superimposes on the right lung field and demonstrably confounds some model outputs (DenseNet effusion and pneumothorax scores fall materially when the tube is inpainted; see measurements/05_classifier_tube_robustness.json).
